blocks.text: Quarterly Update Letter – June 30, 2026
Fund Performance1

blocks.html: For the quarter ending on June 30, 2026, the CIFC J Fund Opportunistic CLO LLC (the “Fund” or “J Fund”) returned +4.25% (net). For context, the broader CLO equity asset class returned +1.59% per Citigroup research. 2 The Fund’s outperformance this quarter reflects our portfolio positioning amid a market backdrop that, while still challenged, showed early signs of improvement. The technical pressures we highlighted last quarter as the primary drivers of CLO equity's underperformance continue to persist today, as the arbitrage continued to remain constrained. That said, we are beginning to see signs of stabilization in the CLO arbitrage, as we detail below.

blocks.html: During the quarter, we continued to acquire distressed CLO BB debt, which accounted for approximately 73% of our new purchases, with the remaining 27% allocated to more traditional CLO BB debt. Notably, this was the second consecutive quarter in which we did not purchase CLO equity, given CLO equity's unattractive relative value compared to CLO BB rated debt. Throughout the quarter, we strategically worked with several collateral managers of our BB and B positions to wind down the CLO transactions ahead of their stated maturity dates, accelerating the return of proceeds to the Fund. Eight of the Fund's BB and B rated positions have been liquidated ahead of their stated maturity or are expected to be in the near term accelerating the realization of value on positions we purchased at a discount to net asset value. In one such case, we purchased a position at $54 in July and worked with the manager to liquidate the transaction ahead of its stated maturity date. Ultimately, we expect to realize a recovery of over $66 in the coming months. Our analysis found that the market's valuation models were understating this position's BB net asset value by nearly 5 points, allowing us to purchase it at a significant discount to its ultimate recovery value. By working with the manager to structure an accelerated wind-down, rather than holding the position to maturity, we expect to realize its value over a substantially shorter horizon. We underwrote this position to a 19.1% IRR at the time of purchase in July; assuming the transaction fully unwinds by January, we now expect the realized IRR could exceed 80%.4

blocks.html: The second quarter brought some resolution to the two shocks that had defined Q1 and did so against the bears. Brent crude fell 31% over the quarter to $69.50/bbl, its steepest quarterly decline since the 2020 crash, as a 60-day US-Iran ceasefire reopened the Strait of Hormuz and drained the war premium that had driven crude to a $126 peak. The rate path moved in the opposite direction and with equal force: an 8-4 April FOMC vote, a hot 3.8% May CPI print, and Kevin Warsh's confirmation as Fed Chair repriced year-end expectations from three cuts at the start of the year to hike odds as high as 47%. Warsh's first meeting cemented the shift - rates were held unanimously, forward guidance was dropped, and the median dot moved to point at a 2026 hike rather than a cut. Despite the volatility, risk assets rallied hard. The S&P 500 rose 15%, its best quarter since 2020, powered by a Q1 earnings season that delivered roughly 25% EPS growth. Credit performed well also: high-yield spreads held near multi-decade tights, closing June at 289bps and averaging 302bps for the year, while Treasury yields stayed elevated and largely range-bound.

blocks.html: Leveraged loans returned +1.89%11 in Q2 but closed the softest first half for the asset class in four years. The weakness was concentrated rather than broad with Software as the epicenter. The average bid on Software loans fell to a YTD low near $85 against roughly $97 for the rest of the market, a 12-point gap that marks the widest of the cycle, with software loans down more than 6% YTD. Quality bifurcation widened alongside it - single-B loans turned negative in June for the first time since February while BB rated loans stayed positive every month of the year and stressed/distressed paper climbed to 12.7% of the market from 8.8% at year-end. Primary activity reflected defense over offense: Q2 volume totaled $224B, down 7% QoQ, and shifted toward amendments, including a record $29.5B of amend-to-extend as sponsors chipped away at the 2028 maturity wall. Software's share of new-issue BSL volume collapsed to roughly 9% YTD from 17.6% in 2025 - the lowest since 2013 - with Healthcare leading issuance for the first time since 2015. The technical bid was thin throughout: true new CLO issuance fell to $33.3B, the slowest since Q4 2023, and investor demand of $34.5B ran at roughly half the typical 2024-25 pace. Defaults, by contrast, eased through the quarter - 1.34% in April, 1.35% in May, and 0.97% in June - as last year's large defaults rolled off the trailing window.

blocks.html: CLO liability spreads retraced through the second quarter, reversing from the March wides as risk appetite recovered following the post-crisis tights that opened the year. AAA through BBB rated CLO tranches now stand flat to modestly tighter versus year-end 2025, as the second quarter rally more than offset the first quarter back-up. BB rated CLO debt was the exception, remaining approximately 40bps wider than year-end levels (515bps versus 475bps)12, the one part of the capital structure where the rally has not fully reversed the earlier widening. Issuance technicals were a partial driver of the spread movement. Second quarter volume totaled approximately $128 billion, with refinancing and reset activity accounting for approximately $95 billion, or 74%, versus approximately $33 billion, or 26%, of true new issuance — the highest refinancing and reset share of total issuance since the first quarter of 2017.

blocks.html: The constructive tone in CLO debt has not fully extended to CLO equity, which continues to face a challenging arbitrage environment. While CLO liability spreads have tightened from their March 31st wides, loan spreads have continued to compress by an even greater degree, driven by persistent demand for performing floating-rate loans from CLOs and other market participants. This dynamic has pushed the share of loans trading above par to elevated levels and has contributed to sharply tighter loan spreads through repricing activity. This arbitrage pressure is reflected in issuance volumes: broadly syndicated loan new issue CLO volume is down 23% through June 30, 202613, relative to the same period last year. We expect this slowdown in new issuance, along with the accompanying reduction in loan demand from newly formed CLOs, to gradually ease spread compression in the loan market over time, though the CLO equity arbitrage remains the key factor to monitor heading into the second half of the year.14

blocks.html: Despite the constructive tone and rally in loan prices in the second quarter, the CLO market continues to price in default rates well beyond anything observed historically — including 2020 and the Global Financial Crisis — when using current market prices as a benchmark for implied defaults. The reality is far more benign: realized defaults have remained contained, and core credit quality across CLO collateral pools remains sound. Median CCC/Caa buckets sit at just 4.6–4.8%15, and OC cushions and MVOCs are broadly stable outside pockets of AI-exposed credits. Junior overcollateralization ratios, an important measure of portfolio quality, remain robust across the portfolio, with cushions well intact; this matters because a breach of the junior overcollateralization test would cause CLO equity to stop collecting its distribution for that period.

Outlook

blocks.html: The CLO arbitrage, or the gap between elevated loan spreads and CLO liability spreads that is paid to CLO equity, has been the principal driver of the negative performance in CLO equity for more than a year, as loan spread compression has eroded the excess spread available to equity holders while liability costs have remained comparatively sticky. The Fund was structured specifically for this dislocation, with a portfolio that has been ramped primarily in distressed CLO debt acquired at discounts to net asset value. Encouragingly, a number of emerging tailwinds, discussed below, could help narrow this arbitrage in the months ahead.
blocks.text: The CLO arbitrage, or the gap between elevated loan spreads and CLO liability spreads that is paid to CLO equity, has been the principal driver of the negative performance in CLO equity for more than a year, as loan spread compression has eroded the excess spread available to equity holders while liability costs have remained comparatively sticky. The Fund was structured specifically for this dislocation, with a portfolio that has been ramped primarily in distressed CLO debt acquired at discounts to net asset value. Encouragingly, a number of emerging tailwinds, discussed below, could help narrow this arbitrage in the months ahead.

items: The first of these tailwinds is the elevated, and potentially still-rising, base rate environment. Persistently high base rates — with the market now pricing in some probability of further hikes — continue to favor floating-rate products, driving incremental demand and higher all-in yields; in our view this is already evident in CLO ETF flows, with JAAA, the largest CLO AAA-rated exchange-traded fund, receiving over $1 billion of inflows in June alone.18 We believe CLO equity stands to benefit as well, since higher base rates increase the interest income collected on the underlying floating-rate loan collateral, boosting the cash flow available to equity after debt service on the liability stack. As this demand builds across the capital structure, we believe it should help compress CLO liability spreads and ease some of the pressure on the arbitrage.

The second tailwind is a meaningful improvement in the capital efficiency of insurer holdings of CLO debt. Under the National Association of Insurance Commissioners' (NAIC) risk-based capital framework, insurers must hold capital against each balance sheet asset sized to that asset's perceived risk; a higher risk-based capital ("RBC") charge requires more capital to be set aside and lowers the effective return on holding the asset.19 The NAIC's agreement to cut RBC charges on insurer holdings of CLO AAA through A rated tranches by 70% to 90% substantially reduces the capital insurers must hold against these tranches, which correspondingly raises the effective, capital- adjusted yield insurers earn on them. This removes a long-standing structural impediment to insurer participation in the CLO market and in our view should support continued, and potentially growing, senior demand going forward.

The challenging arbitrage has already begun to weigh on new issue activity: through June 30, 2026, broadly syndicated loan new issue CLO volumes are down 23% versus the same period in 2025.20 We expect this slowdown in new issue CLO volumes, along with the accompanying reduction in demand for bank loans from newly formed CLOs, to gradually ease spread compression in the loan market and help tighten CLO liability spreads over time.

In our view, one near-term technical headwind bears monitoring: approximately 28% of outstanding AAA CLO paper will be callable by year-end 2026 with coupons at or above 130 basis points, well above current new-issue clearing levels, which stand in the low 120 basis point range.21 As these transactions exit their non-call periods, collateral managers face a clear economic incentive to refinance or reset, and we expect the resulting pipeline of AAA supply to continue pressuring liability spreads in the near term.
